documents.title: Endocrine Society guideline primary aldosteronism case detection

chunks.content: INTRODUCTION Primary aldosteronism is a common, under-recognized cause of secondary hypertension and is present in approximately 5–10% of all hypertensive patients [ , ]. Compared with essential hypertension (EHT), primary aldosteronism is associated with greater cardiovascular risk and target-organ damage, partly attributed to mineralocorticoid receptor–mediated inflammation, fibrosis, and oxidative stress beyond blood-pressure load [ , ]. Cardiac remodeling is a salient downstream consequence of renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS) dysregulation. Patients with primary aldosteronism more often show left ventricular hypertrophy and myocardial fibrosis, often out of proportion to blood pressure; targeted treatment can partially reverse these changes [ ]. Left ventricular mass index (LVMI) is a robust marker of structural remodeling, whereas excess LVMI (eLVMI) quantifies left ventricular mass beyond that predicted by hemodynamic load, capturing maladaptive remodeling associated with adverse outcomes [ ]. Aging strongly shapes morbidity and mortality, but chronological age incompletely reflects inter-individual biological aging [ ]. The Gompertz law–based biological age (GOLD BioAge) model, derived from routine clinical biomarkers – offers a practical estimate of biological age [ ]; GOLD BioAgeDiff (BioAge–chronological age) predicts morbidity and mortality in general populations [ ]. Whether RAAS perturbations in primary aldosteronism are associated with accelerated biological aging, and whether this aging burden tracks cardiac structural remodeling remain unclear [ , ]. We hypothesized that elevated plasma aldosterone concentration (PAC), suppressed plasma renin activity (PRA), and a higher aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR) are associated with higher GOLD BioAgeDiff, which correlates with greater LVMI and eLVMI. METHODS Data sources This study is part of the Study on Primary Aldosteronism in Nanchang (NPAS), which was registered at Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2200057297; https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=133752 ). NPAS is an inpatient hypertension screening cohort established in 2017. The protocol was approved by the Biomedical Research Ethics Committee of the Second Affiliated Hospital of Nanchang University (approval number: 2022-05) and complied with the Declaration of Helsinki; prospective participants provided written informed consent, and retrospective data were de-identified before analysis. Study design, setting, and participants We conducted a retrospective cross-sectional analysis of hypertensive inpatients undergoing standardized evaluation for secondary hypertension at the Second Affiliated Hospital of Nanchang University (Nanchang, China). Clinical information from these routine screenings was curated into the NPAS database. Participants were classified into two groups based on their final diagnosis. The primary aldosteronism group consisted of consecutive patients diagnosed with primary aldosteronism and hospitalized between October 2017 and November 2022. The EHT group was drawn from patients hospitalized for screening between January 2019 and June 2019, in whom secondary causes were excluded. For the primary analysis, patients were excluded if they had missing data on key variables [age, serum creatinine (Scr), plasma glucose (Glu), mean corpuscular volume (MCV), red cell distribution width (RDW), serum albumin (Alb), alkaline phosphatase (ALP), lymphocyte percentage (Lym%), white blood cell count (WBC), and gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT), ARR, or postcaptopril PAC)], had a diagnosis of secondary hypertension other than primary aldosteronism, such as renovascular hypertension due to renal artery stenosis, renal hypertension due to renal parenchymal disease, pheochromocytoma, Cushing syndrome, obstructive sleep apnea, and gestational hypertension. or presented with extreme GOLD BioAge values (1.5 × interquartile range). For echocardiographic analyses, we additionally excluded patients without echocardiography. Diagnosis of primary aldosteronism The diagnosis of primary aldosteronism was made according to the Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline [ ], as previously described in our published work [ ]. Briefly, prior to admission, Patients stopped ARR-interfering medications or switched to verapamil and/or terazosin for 2–4 weeks. An ARR greater than 30 [(ng/dl)/(ng/ml/h)] prompted confirmatory testing (captopril challenge or saline infusion) to diagnose primary aldosteronism. Diagnosis of essential hypertension EHT was defined by office SBP at least 140 mmHg and/or DBP 90 mmHg on repeated inpatient measurements or a documented hypertension history with current treatment [ ], after excluding secondary causes through standardized work-up. Primary aldosteronism was excluded by ARR 30 or less under standardized medication preparation or by negative confirmatory testing when ARR was elevated [ ]. In addition, all secondary causes of hypertension were excluded through the standardized inpatient work-up as described above. Exclusion relied on history and physical examination, routine laboratory testing including renal function and urinalysis, endocrine assays when appropriate, and imaging or functional testing as clinically indicated. The final EHT diagnosis was determined by the treating physicians. Data collection and definitions PAC and PRA were measured by automated chemiluminescence immunoassay (MAGLUMI 4000 Plus) as previously described [ ]. PRA was derived from angiotensin I generation during incubation (4 versus 37 °C), and ARR was calculated as PAC/PRA. For the primary aldosteronism screening test, samples for PAC and PRA were collected after subjects had been in a sitting or standing position for at least 2 h. determined by the treating physicians. Data collection and definitions PAC and PRA were measured by automated chemiluminescence immunoassay (MAGLUMI 4000 Plus) as previously described [ ]. PRA was derived from angiotensin I generation during incubation (4 versus 37 °C), and ARR was calculated as PAC/PRA. For the primary aldosteronism screening test, samples for PAC and PRA were collected after subjects had been in a sitting or standing position for at least 2 h. Clinical data and comorbidity information were obtained from the electronic medical record system and the hospital's central testing laboratory, including sex, age, height, weight, duration of hypertension, SBP, DBP, smoking history, alcohol consumption, MCV, RDW, Alb, ALP, Glu, Lym%, WBC, GGT, serum potassium, serum sodium, total cholesterol (TC), triglycerides, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), Scr, and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). Smoking history was defined as smoking more than one cigarette per day, at least 1 year, or 18 packs per year. Alcohol drinking history was defined as on average, drinking alcohol at least two times a week for more than 1 year. Comorbidities were identified based on discharge diagnoses determined by specialist physicians in accordance with standard clinical guidelines. Outcome The primary outcome was GOLD BioAgeDiff, defined as the difference between the GOLD BioAge and chronological age. GOLD BioAge was calculated using the GOLD BioAge model [ ]: GOLD BioAge = chronological age+ ∑(β i × Biomarker i ) + β 0 (β 0 = −53.6287), where biomarkers were Scr, Glu, MCV, RDW, Alb, ALP, Lym%, WBC, and GGT. GOLD BioAgeDiff was defined as GOLD BioAge − chronological age. The secondary outcomes were LVMI and eLVMI. Doppler echocardiography was used to evaluate the cardiac structure as described previously [ ]. Echocardiography was performed by experienced sonographers blinded to diagnosis using standardized measurements. Two-dimensional and two-dimensionally guided M-mode images were recorded from standardized views. Left ventricular internal diameter in diastole (LVIDd), posterior wall thickness in diastole (PWTd), and interventricular septal thickness in diastole (SWTd) were measured and incorporated into the Devereux-modified formula to estimate left ventricular (LV) mass. LV mass was calculated by the formula: LV mass = 0.8 × {1.04[(LVIDd + PWTd + SWTd) 3 – (LVIDd) 3 ]} + 0.6 (g) [ ]. LVMI was calculated by dividing LV mass by body surface area (BSA). The body surface area was calculated as follow: BSA (m 2 ) = 0.0061 × height (cm) + 0.0128 × weight (kg) − 0.1529 [ ]. Stroke volume was derived using the Teichholz method [ ]. Stroke work was estimated as SBP (mmHg) × stroke volume (ml) × 0.0144 (g m), as previously described [ ]. As simultaneous SBP measurement immediately after echocardiography was not routinely available, we used admission SBP recorded within 48 h of the echocardiographic examination as a surrogate for systolic loading conditions. The predicted LVM was estimated by the equation derived previously: predicted LVM = 55.37 + 6.64 × height (m 2.7 ) + 0.64 × stroke work − 18.07 × sex (where sex was coded as male = 1 and female = 2) [ , ]. Predicted LVMI was then calculated as predicted LVM/BSA. The eLVMI was defined as measured LVMI − predicted LVMI [ ]. Statistical analysis Variables with at least 20% missing data were excluded from the analysis. For those with 20% or less missing values, missing data were imputed using multiple imputation, implemented through the mice package in R. Clinical characteristics were compared between patients with primary aldosteronism and those with EHT. Normally distributed data are presented as mean (SD) and compared using the Student's t test; nonnormally distributed data are summarized as median [IQR] and compared using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. Categorical variables are described as counts (percentages) and compared using the χ 2 test or Fisher's exact test, as appropriate. ARR was log-transformed due to skewed distributions. Multivariable linear regression models were constructed for the primary analysis to evaluate the association of RAAS measures with GOLD BioAgeDiff, and for the secondary analysis to examine the relationship between GOLD BioAgeDiff and LVMI/eLVMI. Covariates were likewise selected a priori based upon clinical knowledge, previous literature, and data availability. For the primary analysis: Model 1 was unadjusted. Model 2 adjusted for sex, age, and BMI. Model 3 further adjusted for SBP, DBP, serum potassium, TC, triglycerides, HDL-C, LDL-C, cardiac insufficiency, peripheral vascular disease, coronary heart disease, atrial fibrillation, stroke, smoking, alcohol, and hypertension duration. For the secondary analysis: Model 1 was unadjusted. Model 2 adjusted for the full set of covariates used in primary Model 3. Model 3 was additionally adjusted for PAC, PRA, and log-ARR. Given the significant interaction between disease subtype (primary aldosteronism versus EHT) and ARR, subgroup analyses were restricted to the primary aldosteronism population. Heterogeneity was assessed using interaction terms. No adjustment for multiple comparisons was

for sex, age, and BMI. Model 3 further adjusted for SBP, DBP, serum potassium, TC, triglycerides, HDL-C, LDL-C, cardiac insufficiency, peripheral vascular disease, coronary heart disease, atrial fibrillation, stroke, smoking, alcohol, and hypertension duration. For the secondary analysis: Model 1 was unadjusted. Model 2 adjusted for the full set of covariates used in primary Model 3. Model 3 was additionally adjusted for PAC, PRA, and log-ARR. Given the significant interaction between disease subtype (primary aldosteronism versus EHT) and ARR, subgroup analyses were restricted to the primary aldosteronism population. Heterogeneity was assessed using interaction terms. No adjustment for multiple comparisons was applied, as these analyses were exploratory and aimed at minimizing type II errors. Mediation analyses were performed using nonparametric bootstrapping with 1000 iterations to examine whether GOLD BioAgeDiff mediates the association between ARR and eLVMI. These models were adjusted for sex, age, BMI, smoking, and alcohol. To compare mediation effects between primary aldosteronism and EHT, a bootstrap-based difference test with 5000 samples was conducted; significance was inferred if the 95% confidence interval (CI) of the average causal mediation effect (ACME) difference (Δ = ACME_PA − ACME_EHT) excluded zero [ ]. All statistical analyses were conducted using R 4.4.2(R Foundation for Computing, Vienna, Austria).Two-tailed P values less than 0.05 was regarded as statistically significant. RESULTS Characteristics of the study population From October 2017 to November 2022, a total of 1053 patients diagnosed with primary aldosteronism were initially screened. In addition, 616 patients with EHT without primary aldosteronism, enrolled between January 2019 and June 2019, were included as a comparison group. After excluding 337 patients with missing data, 117 with concomitant secondary hypertension other than primary aldosteronism, and 14 with extreme GOLD BioAge values, 1201 patients were eligible for primary analysis, including 785 patients with primary aldosteronism and 416 patients with EHT. For the secondary analysis focused on echocardiographic outcomes, a further 92 patients without available echocardiography were excluded, yielding 1109 participants including 717 patients with primary aldosteronism and 392 patients with EHT (Fig. ). Among the 1201 patients included in the primary analysis, the mean age was 49.4 (11.0) years and 687 (57.2%) were men. The mean GOLD BioAge was 57 (13) years, and the mean GOLD BioAgeDiff was 7.6 (4.7) years. Compared with EHT, primary aldosteronism patients had the expected RAAS profile (lower PRA and higher PAC/ARR), were older with longer hypertension duration, and differed in electrolytes, lipids, and comorbidity patterns (Table ). Association between aldosterone, renin, and aldosterone-to-renin ratio and Gompertz law–based biological age difference In the overall cohort, RAAS indices were positively associated with GOLD BioAgeDiff (Table ). In fully adjusted Model 3, PAC, PRA, and postcaptopril PAC showed statistically significant positive associations with GOLD BioAgeDiff (PAC: β = 0.022, 95% CI 0.008–0.035, P = 0.002; PRA: β = 0.110, 95% CI 0.031–0.188, P = 0.006; postcaptopril PAC: β = 0.025, 95% CI 0.009–0.041, P = 0.002), whereas the association for log-transformed ARR was not statistically significant ( β =0.108, 95% CI −0.028 to 0.243, P = 0.120). In stratified analyses by hypertension subtype, distinct association patterns were observed between primary aldosteronism and EHT. Among patients with primary aldosteronism, log-transformed ARR, PAC, and postcaptopril PAC were significantly positively associated with GOLD BioAgeDiff ( β = 0.292, 95% CI 0.076–0.507, P = 0.008; β = 0.015, 95% CI 0.000–0.031, P = 0.049; and β = 0.021, 95% CI 0.004–0.038, P = 0.014, respectively), whereas PRA was not significantly associated ( β = −0.507, 95% CI −1.600 to 0.586, P = 0.363) (Table ). In contrast, among patients EHT, PAC, PRA, and postcaptopril PAC were significantly positively associated with GOLD BioAgeDiff ( β = 0.058, 95% CI 0.022–0.093, P = 0.001; β = 0.126, 95% CI 0.040–0.212, P = 0.004; and β = 0.341, 95% CI 0.060–0.622, P = 0.018, respectively), while log-transformed ARR was not significantly associated ( β = −0.138, 95% CI −0.487 to 0.212, P = 0.440) (Table ). Interaction analyses indicated that hypertension subtype significantly modified the associations of both PAC and log-transformed ARR with GOLD BioAgeDiff (Model 3, P for interaction = 0.014 and 0.032, respectively). No significant interaction was observed for PRA ( P for interaction = 0.196) or postcaptopril PAC ( P for interaction = 0.200) (Table ). Associations of Gompertz law–based biological age difference with left ventricular mass index and excessive left ventricular mass index In the overall cohort, GOLD BioAgeDiff was not significantly associated with eLVMI in any of the three models (all P > 0.05). For LVMI, a significant association was observed in Model 1 ( β = 0.780, 95% CI 0.068–1.492, P = 0.032), but this association was attenuated and became nonsignificant after adjustment in models 2 and 3 (Model 2: P = 0.063; Model 3: P = 0.068) (Table ). Associations of Gompertz law–based biological age difference with left ventricular mass index and excessive left ventricular mass index In the overall cohort, GOLD BioAgeDiff was not significantly associated with eLVMI in any of the three models (all P > 0.05). For LVMI, a significant association was observed in Model 1 ( β = 0.780, 95% CI 0.068–1.492, P = 0.032), but this association was attenuated and became nonsignificant after adjustment in models 2 and 3 (Model 2: P = 0.063; Model 3: P = 0.068) (Table ). In stratified analyses by hypertension subtype, distinct association patterns were observed. Among patients with primary aldosteronism, GOLD BioAgeDiff was significantly positively associated with both eLVMI and LVMI in the fully adjusted model (eLVMI: β = 0.591, 95% CI 0.264–0.917, P < 0.001; LVMI: β = 0.640, 95% CI 0.259–1.021, P = 0.001). In contrast, among patients with EHT, GOLD BioAgeDiff was not significantly associated with either eLVMI ( P = 0.815) or LVMI ( P = 0.474) in Model 3 (Table ). Interaction analyses did not indicate significant effect modification by hypertension subtype for either outcome in Model 3 ( P for interaction = 0.901 for eLVMI and 0.984 for LVMI) (Table ). Mediation analysis In the overall cohort, higher log-ARR was associated with greater GOLD BioAgeDiff (path a: β = 0.129, P = 0.043), and GOLD BioAgeDiff showed a positive but nonsignificant association with eLVMI (path b: β = 0.539, P = 0.235). The direct effect of log-ARR on eLVMI after accounting for GOLD BioAgeDiff was not significant (path c΄: β = 0.740, P = 0.442). The ACME was 0.0696 (95% CI −0.0025 to 0.1780; P = 0.060), corresponding to 8.6% of the total effect being mediated (Fig. ). In patients with primary aldosteronism, associations along the mediation pathway were stronger. Log-ARR was significantly related to GOLD BioAgeDiff (path a: β = 0.257, P = 0.013), and GOLD BioAgeDiff was positively associated with eLVMI (path b: β = 0.538, P = 0.002). The direct effect of log-ARR on eLVMI remained nonsignificant (path c΄: β = 0.504, P = 0.285). GOLD BioAgeDiff significantly mediated the association between log-ARR and eLVMI, with an ACME of 0.1382 (95% CI 0.0248–0.2991; P = 0.008) and a mediated proportion of 21.5%. In contrast, no component of the mediation pathway reached significance in EHT (path a: β = −0.127, P = 0.496; path b: β = 0.569, P = 0.640; path c΄: β = 3.672, P = 0.412). The ACME was −0.0725 (95% CI −0.4942 to 0.1205; P = 0.528), with a proportion mediated of −2.0%. The bootstrap-based difference test showed a difference of ΔACME = 0.2315 (95% CI −0.0257 to 0.6378), which approached statistical significance ( P = 0.080). Subgroup analysis Subgroup analyses revealed a significant interaction only for diabetes ( P for interaction = 0.036). The positive association between log-ARR and bioage_diff was prominent in participants without diabetes ( β = 0.367, 95% CI: 0.133–0.602; P = 0.002) but was not observed in those with diabetes. Across all other subgroups – including age, sex, lifestyle factors, and other cardiovascular comorbidities – the association remained generally consistent, with no significant heterogeneity detected (all P for interaction > 0.05) (Figure S1). DISCUSSION In this cross-sectional study of 785 patients with primary aldosteronism and 416 with EHT, we observed subtype-specific associations between RAAS indices and biological aging. In fully adjusted models, log-ARR was positively associated with GOLD BioAgeDiff in primary aldosteronism but not in EHT ( P for interaction <0.05). In primary aldosteronism, higher GOLD BioAgeDiff was independently associated with higher LVMI and eLVMI. Biological aging clocks have evolved from chronological age-based models to third-generation ’pace of aging’ metrics [ – ]; the GOLD BioAge used in this study aligns with second-generation clocks, which incorporate physiological biomarkers to capture systemic aging and mortality risk [ ]. Although the association between hypertension and biological aging has been explored, direct evidence regarding primary aldosteronism remains limited. PhenoAge is an epigenetic biomarker calculated by weighting DNA methylation levels at 513 CpG sites [ ]. A recent study reported that hypertension was associated with higher PhenoAge ( β = 12, 95% CI 11–13; P < 0.001) and PhenoAge acceleration ( β = 0.56, 95% CI 0.15–0.98; P = 0.009) [ ]. We extend these observations to mineralocorticoid excess in primary aldosteronism. We observed higher GOLD BioAgeDiff in patients with primary aldosteronism compared to those with EHT. In multivariable models, PAC remained associated with higher GOLD BioAgeDiff, and log-ARR was independently associated with GOLD BioAgeDiff specifically in primary aldosteronism. These findings suggest that autonomous aldosterone excess with RAAS dysregulation in primary aldosteronism may contribute to a systemic aging burden beyond blood-pressure load. The association between primary aldosteronism and higher GOLD BioAgeDiff is biologically plausible, although mechanisms cannot be confirmed

We observed higher GOLD BioAgeDiff in patients with primary aldosteronism compared to those with EHT. In multivariable models, PAC remained associated with higher GOLD BioAgeDiff, and log-ARR was independently associated with GOLD BioAgeDiff specifically in primary aldosteronism. These findings suggest that autonomous aldosterone excess with RAAS dysregulation in primary aldosteronism may contribute to a systemic aging burden beyond blood-pressure load. The association between primary aldosteronism and higher GOLD BioAgeDiff is biologically plausible, although mechanisms cannot be confirmed in this cross-sectional study. Primary aldosteronism features autonomous aldosterone excess with renin suppression, leading to chronic mineralocorticoid receptor activation [ ]. Mineralocorticoid receptor activation promotes oxidative stress and sterile inflammation, pro-fibrotic/vascular remodeling, and endothelial dysfunction with microvascular impairment across organs [ ]. Persistent mineralocorticoid receptor activation may induce mitochondrial dysfunction and reactive oxygen species generation, amplifying oxidative stress and inflammation [ ]. This cascade may also intersect with aging biology through Klotho-related pathways [ ]. Clinically, primary aldosteronism is associated with greater arterial stiffness and vascular aging than EHT, supporting blood pressure–independent pro-aging vascular effects of aldosterone [ ]. Furthermore, higher aldosterone exposure has also been associated with shorter leukocyte telomere length, consistent with aldosterone-related cellular senescence [ ]. Because these pathways affect inflammation, metabolism, and organ function, domains captured by the biomarkers in GOLD BioAge, mineralocorticoid receptor-mediated injury may manifest as a higher multisystem ‘aging burden’. This mechanism elucidates the phenomenon observed in our study: after fully adjusting for potential confounding factors, aldosterone-related indices remained independently and positively correlated with GOLD BioAgeDiff. Previous studies have provided strong evidence that accelerated biological aging aligns with structural target-organ damage, including cardiac remodeling. Recently, using UK Biobank data, Mao et al. showed that biological age acceleration, calculated via the the Klemera–Doubal and PhenoAge algorithms [ , ], was associated with adverse cardiac structure and function and a higher risk of incident heart failure; their Mendelian randomization analyses further suggested a potential causal contribution to cardiac remodeling [ ]. Higher ARR has been associated with arterial stiffness, LV hypertrophy, and atrial enlargement, partly independent of blood-pressure load [ ]. eLVMI represents LV mass beyond that predicted by body size and hemodynamic load, and may better reflect maladaptive, nonhemodynamic remodeling [ ]. In primary aldosteronism, GOLD BioAgeDiff was independently associated with LVMI and eLVMI, aligning with Mao et al. [ ] to suggest that systemic aging burden may track aldosterone-related maladaptive remodeling. Mediation analyses further indicated that GOLD BioAgeDiff statistically accounted for part of the log-ARR–eLVMI association, though establishing causality and temporality requires longitudinal and interventional validation. In the subgroup analyses stratified by clinical characteristics, a nominal interaction was observed regarding diabetes status ( P for interaction = 0.036). The positive association between log-ARR and GOLD BioAgeDiff was prominent in participants without diabetes but was not statistically significant in those with concomitant diabetes. Diabetes is a strong driver of oxidative stress and inflammation and may produce a ‘ceiling effect’ that attenuates additional aldosterone-related aging signals [ , ]. Antidiabetic therapies such as metformin, SGLT2 inhibitors may also exert cardiometabolic benefits that modify RAAS-related injury signals [ – ]. Because subgroup analyses were exploratory and the diabetic subgroup was smaller, this interaction should be considered hypothesis-generating and requires confirmation. Methodologically, we used the complete GOLD BioAge model rather than Light BioAge because C-reactive protein required for the simplified model was not routinely measured [ ]. Additionally, the complete model includes immune cell, erythrocyte, and hepatobiliary indices that may better capture primary aldosteronism-related multisystem attrition [ , – ]. Because GOLD BioAge was developed in Western general populations, calibration in Chinese primary aldosteronism cohorts warrants evaluation. Nevertheless, applying the same algorithm across groups supports internal comparisons even if absolute biological age values shift systematically. GOLD BioAgeDiff is readily computed from routine laboratory indices and may serve as a quantitative phenotype of multisystem burden in primary aldosteronism. Its association with LVMI/eLVMI suggests potential utility for refined risk stratification and prioritizing cardiac assessment. Future prospective and interventional studies are required to validate its clinical applicability, optimal thresholds, and reversibility following primary aldosteronism-specific treatment. This study has several limitations. First, the cross-sectional design limits inference to associations and precludes causal conclusions. Second, this single-center inpatient cohort may be subject to selection bias and limited generalizability. Third, stroke work was estimated using admission SBP within 48 h rather than contemporaneous SBP at echocardiography, potentially introducing nondifferential measurement error in predicted LVM/eLVMI that may bias associations toward the null. Fourth, residual confounding is possible because detailed lifestyle data, including dietary patterns and sleep quality, and long-term use of nonantihypertensive medications, including lipid-lowering and antidiabetic agents, were unavailable, despite standardized medication washout before RAAS profiling. First, the cross-sectional design limits inference to associations and precludes causal conclusions. Second, this single-center inpatient cohort may be subject to selection bias and limited generalizability. Third, stroke work was estimated using admission SBP within 48 h rather than contemporaneous SBP at echocardiography, potentially introducing nondifferential measurement error in predicted LVM/eLVMI that may bias associations toward the null. Fourth, residual confounding is possible because detailed lifestyle data, including dietary patterns and sleep quality, and long-term use of nonantihypertensive medications, including lipid-lowering and antidiabetic agents, were unavailable, despite standardized medication washout before RAAS profiling. These limitations indicate that our conclusions require confirmation in larger and more rigorous studies. In conclusion, in a single-center inpatient hypertension screening cohort, GOLD BioAgeDiff was higher in patients with primary aldosteronism compared to those with EHT. Within the primary aldosteronism population, log-ARR, PAC, and postcaptopril PAC were independently and positively associated with GOLD BioAgeDiff; furthermore, GOLD BioAgeDiff was independently associated with LVMI and eLVMI, suggesting that it may partially mediate the association between ARR and eLVMI. These findings implicate a link between primary aldosteronism-related RAAS imbalance, accelerated biological aging, and cardiac remodeling, although causality and reversibility remain to be further verified by longitudinal and interventional studies. documents.title: Endocrine Society guideline diagnosis treatment hyperprolactinemia

chunks.content: CASE 1 In February 2019, a male patient aged 40 years was referred to a neurologist because of intense and recurrent headaches. Among the examinations performed to investigate the headaches, the brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans showed an intrasellar pituitary microadenoma 8 × 6 × 8 mm in size (tumor volume, 1.96 cm 3 ). The patient was then referred for endocrinological advice. Medical history revealed that the patient was the father of 2 children aged 4 years and 2 years, respectively. Decreased libido and erectile dysfunction occurred over the past year. At the first endocrinological assessment, pituitary function investigation revealed hyperprolactinemia (prolactin [PRL], 900 µg/L; normal range, 5-20 µg/L) and concomitant hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (FSH, 1.1 IU/mL; LH, 1.3 IU/mL; testosterone, 175 ng/dL). A concomitant seminal fluid examination revealed the presence of mild oligospermia, whereas at the dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry scan bone mineral density was normal. Therefore, the diagnosis of pituitary microadenoma with hyperprolactinemia was given, and cabergoline therapy was started at the dose of 1 mg/wk. The clinical course was indolent over the following 6 months and responsiveness to cabergoline was acceptable, with a significant decrease in PRL levels (180 µg/L, Δ = −80%), together with a reduction in the headache intensity and frequency and an improvement in libido and erectile function. Therefore, given that PRL levels were progressively decreasing, the treatment with cabergoline was maintained at the same dose. CASE 2 In December 2009, a woman aged 26 years was referred to endocrinological consultation for infertility. Medical history revealed oligo-amenorrhea and mild hirsutism (Ferriman–Gallway score = 9) over the past 10 years, associated with progressive weight gain in the past 3 years. At the gynecological ultrasounds performed over several years, the ovaries displayed a multifollicular aspect with no clear evidence of polycystic ovary syndrome, whereas hormonal assessment revealed normal androgen levels associated with mild hyperprolactinemia (up to 36 µg/L; normal range, 5 -25 µg/L). The patient had received treatment with oral contraceptives for 2 years, from 2004 to 2006, with rapid relapse of the clinical syndrome after the oral contraceptives were withdrawn. At the first endocrinological assessment, the patient reported amenorrhea over the past 9 months, recurrent headaches, and moderate hyperprolactinemia (PRL, 126.7 µg/L). A pituitary MRI scan was performed and revealed a microadenoma of 8 mm maximal diameter. The patient's facial characteristics (prominent frontal and zygomatic bones, enlarged nose, and mandibular prognathism) were suggestive of concomitant GH hypersecretion, but GH and IGF-I levels were within the normal range (GH, 0.3 µg/L; IGF-I, 206 µg/L). Therefore, the diagnosis of pituitary microadenoma with hyperprolactinemia was carried out, and cabergoline therapy was started at the dose of 0.5 mg/wk. The clinical course was indolent over the years and responsiveness to cabergoline was optimal, with complete PRL normalization (PRL, 18 µg/L), and a 50% shrinkage in pituitary tumor size, associated with full recovery of the clinical syndrome. In November 2016, the pituitary MRI scan revealed a 50% increase in maximal tumor diameter, from 3 to 6 mm, suggesting tumor regrowth. PRL levels slightly increased to 28 µg/L, thus requiring an increase in cabergoline dose to 1 mg/wk. One year later, PRL remained stable at 27 µg/L and pituitary MRI scans revealed a 25% decrease in maximal tumor diameter, but the patient reported persistent headache and asthenia. In September 2018, the patient was discovered to be pregnant; therefore, cabergoline was promptly withdrawn. The patient underwent regular endocrinological controls during gestation; no impairment in the visual field was recorded, and a term delivery without maternal and fetal complications occurred in March 2019. The patient skipped postpartum controls for 1 year during breastfeeding and required new endocrinological consultation only in March 2020, when the first PRL assessment 4 months after cessation of breastfeeding result was as high as 30.7 µg/L. CASE 3 In November 2004, a male patient aged 35 years was referred to ophthalmologic consultation because of the occurrence of visual disturbances, particularly the narrowing of the visual field. Concomitant visual field examination revealed bitemporal hemianopsia. Medical history revealed that the patient was the father of 2 children aged 6 years and 4 years, respectively. Decreased libido and frequent headaches occurred over the past 3 years and were associated with weight gain in the past 5 years. Accounting for approximately 40% of the entire cohort of pituitary tumors, prolactinomas are the most common hormone-secreting pituitary adenomas; infertility and gonadal and sexual dysfunction are the most relevant clinical features in both sexes ( ). Prolactinomas are the main pathologic cause of PRL excess, albeit several different conditions may induce the increase in PRL levels and should be excluded before a diagnosis is made ( ). In clinical practice, microprolactinomas (<10 mm in size) are more frequent than macroprolactinomas (>10 mm in size) and occur more frequently in women, in whom the disturbances of the menstrual cycle and infertility generally prompt rapid medical advice leading to an early diagnosis, as in clinical case 2. Conversely, in men the rate of macroprolactinomas with visual field defects, as in clinical case 3, and hypopituitarism at first presentation is higher ( ) and the mean age at diagnosis is at least 10 years delayed compared with women ( ), given that the most important components of the clinical syndrome are the decrease of libido and/or erectile dysfunction, as in clinical case 3. In adults, the estimated prevalence of prolactinomas accounts for 60 to 100 per million population ( , , ). According to a recent review study including different patient series ( ), where standardized incidence rates for pituitary tumors range from 4 to 7.39 cases per 100,000/y, prolactinomas have been reported to represent 40% to 66% of all pituitary tumors ( ). Patient age has been shown to differently influence incidence rates in men and women: indeed, between the age of 20 and 50 years, the ratio between women and men is estimated to be 10:1, whereas after the sixth decade of life, the frequency of prolactinomas is similar in both sexes ( ). This difference may reflect that in young females the clinical syndrome resulting from hypogonadism (infertility and oligo-amenorrhea) prompts early medical advice, particularly in case of pregnancy desire. Conversely, in elderly patients, including postmenopausal women, and in men, the diagnosis is due predominantly to mass effects from large tumors. In pediatric and adolescent ages, prolactinomas, albeit rare, represent about 50% of all pituitary tumors ( , ). THE INTERPLAY BETWEEN PROLACTIN AND FERTILITY Hyperprolactinemia is the most common cause of secondary hypogonadism and infertility in both sexes. In infertile women, PRL excess as the main cause of infertility has been found to vary from 7% to 20% of cases, being lower than that reported in women with amenorrhea and/or galactorrhea, but at least 10-fold higher than that of the general population ( ). The impact of PRL excess on the reproductive axis reflects its peculiar actions at both the central and peripheral levels ( ). At the central level, PRL modulates the reproductive axis by directly suppressing kisspeptin secretion, thus lowering GnRH activation and gonadotropins secretion, so promoting hypogonadism and infertility ( , ). At the peripheral level, PRL plays a direct inhibitory effect on sexual hormone synthesis and secretion. In women, PRL inhibits estrogen and progesterone synthesis ( ). APPROACH TO PATIENT IDENTIFICATION Predisposition Although most pituitary adenomas occur in a sporadic setting, prolactinomas may arise from germline genetic mutations predisposing to pituitary tumor development in the context of some inherited syndromes ( ). The association with genetic defects may result in more aggressive clinical behavior and poor responsiveness to standard treatment with dopamine agonists (DA). Particularly, in the context of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN-1) and type 4 (MEN-4), and familial isolated pituitary adenomas, prolactinomas are the most frequent pituitary tumor histotype. Overall, the efficacy of DA has been documented in 51.5% of prolactinomas within MEN-1 ( ), but responsiveness to DA has been not consistently reported across studies ( ), varying from a scant ( , ) to a good response to DA ( ), and from an aggressive ( , ) to an indolent tumor clinical behavior leading to occasional tumor growth without clinical consequences ( ). To a similar extent, in the context of MEN-4 and familial isolated pituitary adenomas, prolactinomas are larger, more invasive, and less responsive to DA than their sporadic counterparts ( ), suggesting a more aggressive clinical behavior as compared with sporadic tumors. In the context of Carney complex (CNC), prolactinomas are rare, but histology may reveal somatomammotroph hyperplasia leading to the development of GH- and/or PRL-secreting adenomas. In fact, concomitant GH and PRL hypersecretion has been shown to occur in up to 64% of patients with CNC ( ). Concomitant GH and PRL hypersecretion may occur independently in CNC, and the development of acromegaly in patients with a known prolactinoma is rare. Altogether, these findings suggest that for those individuals with prolactinomas who are at risk for carrying a genetic mutation already diagnosed in a relative, genetic screening should be offered after appropriate counseling and an explanation of the potential benefits deriving from early diagnosis ( ). Clinical Presentation at Diagnosis Clinical features of prolactinomas are summarized in . The pituitary adenoma per se may exert several compressive mass effects, resulting in headache, visual field defects, and hypopituitarism ( , ). Prolactin excess results in both sexes in weight gain, delayed pubertal development, hypogonadism, infertility, galactorrhea, and osteopenia or osteoporosis ( , ). Increased PRL levels underpin infertility in 7% to 20% of women and 2% to 4% of men ( ). Other signs and symptoms are gender-related and include, in men, libido reduction, erectile dysfunction, and gynecomastia and, in women, oligo-amenorrhea, vaginal dryness, irritability, and depression ( , ). Particularly in women, the classical amenorrhea–galactorrhea syndrome generally encourages rapid medical consultation, as in clinical case 2, whereas weak symptoms of impotence and decreased libido in men might be frequently underestimated, as in clinical case 1, leading to a diagnostic delay ( ), as in clinical case 3. However, different pathogenesis in men and women has also been hypothesized because rapidly growing prolactinomas with increased markers of cellular proliferation have been reported to occur more frequently in men ( , ). These findings have raised the question of whether prolactinomas are more aggressive in men than in women, but the available evidence is still controversial. In men, prolactinomas are usually large and invasive, with signs and symptoms of hypogonadism and mass effects being the most frequent clinical features ( ). Additionally, according to the last World Health Organization classification ( ), lactotroph tumors in men have a high probability of recurrence because of increased mitotic count and Ki-67 leading to elevated proliferative activity, or plurihormonal PIT-1–positive immunostaining. The latter identifies tumors composed of a monomorphous population of poorly differentiated cells displaying various levels of immunoreactivity for several pituitary tropines, including PRL and GH, β-TSH, and α-subunit, and likely belonging to the acidophilic lineage of adenomas ( ). These PIT-1 immunoreactive adenomas belonging to the acidophilic lineage display an intrinsic aggressive behavior and a high degree of invasiveness, low rates of disease-free survival, and a high propensity for recurrence ( ). Besides the hypogonadism-related signs and symptoms, PRL excess may exert extragonadal systemic effects. Given the direct actions of PRL and dopaminergic tone on pancreatic β cells and adipocytes, hyperprolactinemia may also induce an unfavorable metabolic profile. Increased food intake and weight gain in patients with prolactinomas have been shown to promote altered body composition, insulin resistance, impaired glucose tolerance, and adverse lipid profile, leading to visceral obesity and metabolic syndrome in approximately one-third of patients ( ). However, the potential impact of hyperprolactinemia-induced hypogonadism on body composition and metabolic profile cannot be excluded. Indeed, men with testosterone and dihydrotestosterone levels in the lower quartiles have been found to have a 2-fold higher risk of developing obesity and metabolic syndrome ( ). Similarly, in 40 premenopausal hyperprolactinemic women, in whom FSH, LH, and estrogen levels were in the normal range, but their pulsatile secretion was decreased because of hyperprolactinemia, PRL excess has been found associated with hyperinsulinemia and insulin resistance independently of body weight and leptin and adiponectin levels ( ). The altered body composition, characterized by increased fat mass and reduced lean mass ( , ), together with concomitant secondary hypogonadism, contribute to decreased bone density from the direct and indirect (ie, hyperprolactinemia-induced hypogonadism) effects of prolactin on bone physiology, early alterations in bone turnover markers, reduced bone mass mainly in trabecular rather than cortical bone, delayed peak bone mass acquisition, and high risk of vertebral fractures in both sexes ( ). DIAGNOSTIC APPROACH The diagnostic workup for hyperprolactinemia is shown in . As reported in , a number of physiologic (pregnancy, breastfeeding, stress, exercise, food intake, and sleep) and pathologic conditions (chronic kidney and liver failure, primary hypothyroidism, compression of the pituitary stalk by a non–PRL-secreting pituitary tumor or different parasellar mass, and granulomatous infiltration of the hypothalamus), as well as several drugs (mainly antidepressants, dopamine receptor blockers, dopamine synthesis inhibitors, oral contraceptives, gastrointestinal medications, neuroleptics, and antipsychotics) can induce symptomatic hyperprolactinemia ( , ). Before a correct diagnosis of hyperprolactinemia is made, such conditions must be investigated and excluded. Attention should be paid to medical history, concomitant medications, and biochemical assessment ( , ). This is particularly true in the case of modest PRL elevations, which only occasionally may mask the presence of a prolactinoma ( ), as in clinical case 2. To ascertain the diagnosis of a PRL-secreting pituitary tumor, a single measurement of serum PRL without excessive venipuncture stress is strongly recommended ( ). Breast examination in patients with galactorrhea should not be performed immediately before PRL assessment because any nipple stimulation might result in PRL increase. A level above the upper limit of normal (25 μg/L in women, 20 μg/L in men) raises diagnostic suspicion ( , ). Conversely, dynamic testing of PRL secretion based on the administration of TRH, L-dopa, nomifensine, and domperidone does not find clinical application currently ( ). In uncertain conditions, sampling can be repeated after overnight fasting on a different day in 2 to 3 samples in time course at 15- to 20-minute intervals to minimize the effect of PRL pulsatile secretion ( ). PRL levels >250 μg/L generally confirm the diagnosis of prolactinoma, albeit PRL increase over 200 μg/L can be also seen in case of non–PRL-secreting tumor mass, such as nonfunctioning pituitary tumors ( , ). In presence of a serum PRL level >500 μg/L, the diagnosis of macroprolactinoma can be ruled in ( ). Once other causes of hyperprolactinemia (see previous section) have been excluded, a radiological confirmation with pituitary imaging, mainly based on gadolinium-enhanced MRI is required ( ). Over the past 20 years, pituitary MRI has progressively replaced computed tomography with IV contrast enhancement because the latter is less effective than MRI in visualizing small tumors on the one hand and in shaping the extension of large or giant tumors on the other ( ). Nowadays, a pituitary computed tomography scan is recommended only when MRI is unavailable or contraindicated, such as in patients with cardiac pacemakers, implanted cardiac defibrillators; internal pacing wires; clips for cerebral, carotid, or aortic aneurysm; cochlear implants; any implant held in by magnet; Swan-Ganz catheter; and pregnancy ( ). CHALLENGES IN DIAGNOSIS The “Hook Effect” Diagnostic workup for prolactinomas may be tangled by several challenges. The maximal diameter of the prolactinoma reportedly correlates with PRL levels at baseline ( ). Therefore, in case of discrepancy between a very large pituitary tumor (>3 cm in size) and a modestly increased PRL level, a 1:100 serum sample dilution is recommended to investigate and overcome a laboratory artifact responsible for falsely low PRL levels, namely the “hook effect” ( ). This phenomenon commonly occurs with the use of some immunoassays, such as the 2-site monoclonal “sandwich” assay ( ). The term “hook effect” refers to the typical shape of the binding curve, which goes up as long as the analyte concentrations gradually increase in the sample, but at some critical point exceeding the capacity of the assay components, it turns down ( ). The hook effect may therefore mask a prolactinoma and suggest the incorrect diagnosis of a nonfunctioning pituitary tumor ( ). Of note, current assay methodologies are mainly based on 2-site immunometric assays, which are more sensitive and specific than previous competitive assays but are also susceptible to some interferences such as the high-dose hook effect ( ). Sandwich assays, generally performed in 2 steps or by diluting the samples, are able to avoid this interference, so now the high-dose hook effect persists in a very small minority of PRL assays ( ). Nevertheless, consideration of the hook effect should be taken in PRL assay recommendations ( ). Macroprolactin Macroprolactin is an isoform of PRL with greater molecular weight and reduced biological activity. In patients with asymptomatic hyperprolactinemia, the assessment for macroprolactin can help endocrinologists in preventing incorrect diagnoses leading to inappropriate treatments, and in discriminating true hyperprolactinemia requiring a proper therapeutic approach ( , ). Although more than 80% of circulating PRL is monomeric (23 kDa), serum can also contain a covalently bound dimer and a larger polymeric form, known as “big prolactin” (50 kDa) and “big-big prolactin” (150 kDa), respectively ( , ). In most cases, macroprolactin is composed of a complex formed by an IgG and a monomeric PRL ( , ); consequent hyperprolactinemia results from low renal PRL clearance and reduced dopaminergic tone ( ). Macroprolactin is quite common; it has been reported to cause hyperprolactinemia in approximately 20% of cases ( ). Therefore, screening for macroprolactin with the use of polyethylene glycol should be routinely offered, before investigating alternative causes of PRL excess, in patients with asymptomatic hyperprolactinemia ( , ). The overall prevalence of signs and symptoms of PRL excess in patients with macroprolactin is generally lower than that observed in patients with monomeric hyperprolactinemia ( ). Indeed, menstrual disturbances, including both oligomenorrhea and amenorrhea, as well as galactorrhea and a combination of menstrual disturbances and galactorrhea have been reported to occur in 24%, 13%, and 2% of patients with macroprolactin, respectively, presumably resulting from concomitant disorders, such as polycystic ovary syndrome and pituitary tumors, compared with 26%, 29%, and 34% of those with monomeric hyperprolactinemia, respectively ( ). This suggests a potential overlap in the clinical presentation mainly in terms of infertility features ( ). Of note, more than 60% of patients with macroprolactin reported no peculiar signs and symptoms of PRL excess ( ). The coexistence of macroprolactin and pituitary incidentalomas may result in a further diagnostic pitfall leading to an improper diagnosis of prolactinoma ( ), but the absence of a clinical syndrome specifically ascribable to hyperprolactinemia may assist in a better diagnostic definition ( ). Diagnosis at Menopausal Age Menopause is associated with a physiologic decline of the stimulatory effects of estrogens on PRL secretion and lactotroph cell proliferation and a physiological reduction in circulating PRL levels ( ). Therefore, in postmenopausal women, when fertility does not represent a foremost concern, the lack of the classical amenorrhea–galactorrhea syndrome from PRL excess may result in the underestimation of the exact prevalence of prolactinomas ( ). This is particularly true for women with microprolactinomas, although at least one-third of those diagnosed at menopausal age have reported secondary amenorrhea in their medical history ( ), suggesting that a scrupulous investigation of these symptoms during fertile age might prompt an earlier diagnosis ( ). Most patients (92%) with prolactinomas diagnosed after menopause have been found to harbor a pituitary macroadenoma, or even a giant pituitary tumor ( ), leading predominantly to signs and symptoms of mass effect, such as headache and visual loss, with pituitary apoplexy occurring in approximately 5% of cases ( ). The evidence of large tumor size and frequent invasiveness of prolactinomas in postmenopausal women has raised the question of whether these tumors are biologically comparable with those of male patients ( ), likewise characterized by rapid growth rate and increased markers of cellular proliferation ( , ). However, a lower estrogen receptor α expression, together with low estrogen production, may per se promote lactotroph cell proliferation and trigger the development of large, invasive pituitary tumors in postmenopausal women ( ). Aggressive and Malignant Prolactinomas Lactotroph tumors are the second-most frequent aggressive and malignant tumors ( ). According to the last World Health Organization classification of pituitary tumors ( ), pituitary adenomas have been renamed with the term pituitary neuroendocrine tumors (PitNET) in replacement of adenomas, and specific clinical, pathological, and radiological characteristics have been proposed to identify aggressive and malignant PitNET, including prolactinomas. In this light, attention should be paid to tumor invasiveness and proliferation. Invasion is defined on the basis of histological and/or radiological evidence of cavernous or sphenoid sinus invasion, whereas proliferation is defined on the basis of a mitotic count >2/10 HPF, Ki-67 ≥ 3%, and >10 p53 strongly positive nuclei/10 HPF ( ). Lactotroph tumors developing in patients aged younger than 20 years, mainly in males, and/or with a genetic predisposition have generally a poor prognosis because of a larger size, more frequent invasiveness, and overt resistance to DA ( ), leading to a high risk of recurrence and malignancy. Densely granulated PIT-1–positive PRL-secreting pituitary tumors, mixed somatotroph–lactotroph tumors, and pluri-hormonal PIT-1–positive acidophilic stem cell tumors (tumors of lactotroph differentiation often associated with hyperprolactinemia) are generally more invasive than sparsely granulated variants and less responsive to conventional medical therapy with DA, with overall reduced cure rates ( ). The expression of proliferation markers (Ki-67 expression ≥3%, mitotic count >2) is also correlated with tumor invasiveness and proliferation ( ). Low estrogen receptor α expression and high vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and epidermal growth factor expression are similarly correlated to tumor aggressiveness, and the expression of some adhesion molecules such as E-cadherin, matrix metalloproteinase 9, and abnormalities in chromosomes 1, 11, and 19 has also been correlated with tumor aggressiveness ( , ). As for all PitNET subtypes, according to pathological and/or radiological findings ( ), lactotroph tumors can be classified based on a 5 degree-scale as: noninvasive and nonproliferative (grade 1a); noninvasive and proliferative (grade 1b); invasive and nonproliferative (grade 2a); invasive and proliferative (grade 2b); and metastatic tumor (grade 3). Based on this classification, grade 2b (aggressive) lactotroph tumors have a 20 times higher risk of progression compared with grade 1a tumors ( ). As for aggressive lactotroph tumors, malignant prolactinomas are the second most frequent malignant pituitary tumors after ACTH-secreting pituitary carcinomas ( ). The exact incidence of PRL-secreting carcinomas is yet to be clearly defined, as with that of all pituitary carcinomas, which are known to be very rare (<0.2% of all pituitary tumors). According to the recent European Society surveys ( , ), malignant prolactinomas have been reported to account for approximately 9% of patients with aggressive and malignant pituitary tumors. The definition of malignant prolactinomas parallels that of all pituitary carcinomas and requires the confirmation of distant cerebrospinal, meningeal, and/or systemic metastases ( ). APPROACH TO PATIENT MANAGEMENT Before DA became accessible for medical therapy, surgery and/or radiation therapy were the treatment approaches of choice for prolactinomas ( ). The introduction of DA in the therapeutic algorithm for prolactinomas totally changed the natural course of these tumors, offering a successful treatment strategy that progressively substituted surgery and radiotherapy in routine clinical management ( ). DA, mainly cabergoline, are now recommended as the treatment of choice to lower PRL levels, decrease tumor size, and restore gonadal function for patients harboring PRL-secreting tumors, regardless of tumor size ( , , , ). However, multimodal therapy also including surgery and/or radiotherapy may be required in patients resistant to DA or for those with aggressive prolactinomas ( ). Indications to Treat Patients With Hyperprolactinemia The goals of treatment for prolactinomas include PRL normalization, decrease in tumor size and restoration of gonadal function ( , , , ). In patients with prolactinomas, effective treatments result in relief from the effects of tumor mass, including hypopituitarism, visual field defects, headaches, and cranial nerve palsy; and relief from the effects of PRL excess, including hypogonadism, infertility, and osteopenia/osteoporosis ( ). Noteworthy, asymptomatic patients with microprolactinomas do not categorically require treatment ( , ) because these tumors rarely grow over years ( ). Conversely, independently of tumor size, the presence of a clinical syndrome of PRL excess support the introduction of PRL-lowering therapy ( , ). However, hypogonadal premenopausal women with microadenomas without pregnancy desire may benefit from oral contraceptives/sex hormone replacement instead of dopamine agonists ( ). Caution should be paid to periodic evaluation of PRL levels and potential growth of microadenomas following treatment with oral estrogen therapy, albeit no clear evidence of tumor enlargement after estrogen therapy has been provided so far ( ). The presence of a macroadenoma represents per se a strong indication of treatment, given the known propensity of these tumors to grow ( ). Additional indications for treatment include tumor invasiveness and compression of adjacent structures, such as pituitary stalk or optic chiasm ( , ). Medical Treatment

Medical Treatment of Prolactinomas: Dopamine Agonists Effects on PRL excess, tumor mass and gonadal status DAs represent the recommended treatment to achieve therapeutic goals ( , , ). The use of DA is based on the intrinsic property of dopamine to bind type 2 dopamine receptors (D2DR), which are G-coupled receptor proteins whose activation is able to suppress PRL secretion in the pituitary lactotrophs, as well as PRL gene expression and lactotroph proliferation ( ). Among DA, bromocriptine and cabergoline are the most commonly used compounds in clinical practice worldwide, whereas pergolide, quinagolide, and lisuride are less frequently used or no longer available ( ). Cabergoline is strongly recommended as the treatment of choice for prolactinomas of any size, given the proven greater efficacy over different DA either in PRL normalization and tumor shrinkage ( , ), although head-to-head comparison studies among different DA formulations are still limited. In patients with microprolactinomas and macroprolactinomas, cabergoline has been reported to induce PRL normalization and tumor shrinkage in 95% and 80%, respectively ( ). Regardless of tumor size, PRL normalization has been accomplished in 76% of patients treated with bromocriptine, 87% of those treated with pergolide and 89% of those treated with cabergoline ( ). While on cabergoline, tumor shrinkage has been shown to occur in 60% of patients previously treated with other DA ( ). A similar biochemical and tumoral effectiveness of cabergoline has been documented also in patients of pediatric and adolescent ages ( , ). Following treatment with cabergoline, amenorrhea, infertility, galactorrhea, and sexual dysfunction have been reported to improve in 82%, 53%, 86%, and 67%, respectively, of women with prolactinomas ( , ). The rapid amelioration of women's fertility justifies the advice to use mechanical contraception in patients without pregnancy desire ( , ). Hypogonadism may persist only in a minority of women with prolactinomas and may require replacement treatment ( , ). Symptomatic hyperprolactinemic hypogonadal women may be cautiously administered estrogens/progesterone therapy but careful periodic observation is recommended, although a negative outcome on tumor size has not been documented to date ( ). In men receiving cabergoline, hypogonadism, seminal fluid parameters (sperm count and volume), decreased libido and erectile dysfunction have been reported to improve in 60%, 100%, and 61% of cases, respectively ( ). However, restoration of normal testosterone may not be sufficient to correct sexual dysfunction and seminal abnormalities, thus requiring testosterone replacement therapy ( , , ). In these patients, attention should be paid to specific side effects of improper testosterone replacement treatment, such as aggressiveness, hypersexuality, polycythemia, and prostate enlargement, generally caused by excessive dosages and thus compelling proper dose adjustment ( ). While on testosterone replacement therapy, potential testosterone aromatization to estrogen may occur, virtually stimulating the proliferation and hyperplasia of lactotroph cells in the pituitary and inducing resistance to dopamine agonists ( ). In case of persistent hypogonadism despite PRL normalization following treatment with dopamine agonists, clomiphene citrate may represent an option to improve sperm quality and restore fertility ( ). Effects on Metabolic Profile Additional extrapituitary and extragonadal effects of medical therapy with cabergoline mainly include a metabolic gain ( ). Long-term treatment with cabergoline has been demonstrated to ameliorate or even recover metabolic consequences of PRL excess and hypogonadism ( , , ), such as altered body composition, insulin resistance, impaired glucose tolerance, and adverse lipid profile, which is known to trigger visceral obesity and metabolic syndrome ( ). Long-term treatment with cabergoline has been shown to significantly reduce body weight, body mass index, and waist circumference, thus improving visceral obesity ( ). However, independently of the reduction in body weight, the impact on visceral obesity is supported by the direct beneficial effects of DA on glucose metabolism, insulin resistance, and lipid fractions. Indeed, both bromocriptine and cabergoline have been reported to induce a significant improvement in glucose metabolism and insulin resistance after 6 months of treatment for prolactinomas ( , , ). Particularly, cabergoline significantly reduced fasting insulin and homeostatic model assessment for insulin resistance in prolactinomas, predominantly when used at doses higher than 0.5 mg/wk ( , ). Conversely, the use of a high-dose cabergoline schedule did not remarkably improve lipid metabolism, whereas pituitary surgery was able to significantly reduce total cholesterol and triglycerides ( ), suggesting that lipid fractions might be affected more markedly by the rapid correction of PRL excess rather than by DA. The direct consequence of the metabolic advantage induced by DA is a reduction by 20% in the prevalence of metabolic syndrome ( , , , ). Safety and Tolerability Over the years, the longer half-life and the reduced incidence of side effects contributed to progressively enhancing the use of cabergoline in preference to other DA in clinical practice. Adverse effects of cabergoline are generally less frequent, less severe, and of shorter duration compared with other DA ( ), and mainly include nausea or vomiting, headache, dizziness, vertigo, and arterial hypotension ( , ). Noteworthy, DA use has been found to be associated, albeit rarely, with the occurrence of compulsive behavior and psychosis. Particularly, even at low doses, bromocriptine has been reported to induce mania in postpartum women and induce psychotic reactions in patients with preexisting mental disorders ( ). Conversely, similar findings have been very occasionally reported following treatment with cabergoline ( ). Based on this evidence, the use of DA to achieve normal PRL levels in patients with antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinemia is still questionable because DA might exacerbate underlying psychosis ( ). Given the high binding affinity of cabergoline for serotonin receptor subtype 2B, whose activation reportedly promotes fibroblast proliferation and mitogenesis at the cardiac valve level ( , ), over the past 15 years several independent studies ( ) have investigated the potential association between the use of cabergoline and the development of clinically relevant cardiac valve disease in patients with prolactinomas, as previously demonstrated in patients with Parkinson disease ( ). Noteworthy, the experience collected in patients with Parkinson disease has demonstrated that cardiac valve disease occurred in 29% to 39% of patients, usually receiving cabergoline at doses as high as 3 to 5 mg/d and mean weekly doses up to 25 mg and taking median cumulative doses ranging from 2600 to 6700 mg ( ). Conversely, standard doses of cabergoline routinely used for patients with prolactinomas do not exceed 2 mg/wk in most cases, and only a minority of patients require higher doses to achieve disease control. A recent meta-analysis investigating the prevalence of cardiac valvulopathy did not confirm a similar association and found no significant increase in the prevalence of any valvular disease in patients with hyperprolactinemia receiving cabergoline at standard doses compared with controls, apart from a slight increase in mild (ie, nonclinically relevant) tricuspid regurgitation ( ). Resistant and Aggressive Prolactinomas According to international guidelines ( ), resistance to DA occurs in case of failure to achieve PRL normalization and at least ≥50% reduction in tumor size at maximally tolerated doses. Following treatment with DA, some patients may display discordant responses because PRL normalization may be not associated with a reduction in tumor size or vice versa ( ); other patients may display partial responsiveness and require higher than standard doses of DA to achieve a satisfactory response ( ). However, the definition of resistance to DA is still open to question because there is no full consensus about the definition of the DA dose to which the drug should be up-titrated before classifying a patient as resistant to DA ( ), and specifically, if this dose should be ≥2.0 mg/wk for cabergoline and ≥15 mg/d for bromocriptine ( ). Primary resistance to DA in prolactinomas is rare, accounting for 20% to 30% of patients treated with bromocriptine and nearly 10% to 20% of those receiving cabergoline ( , ). Secondary resistance to DA has been seldom reported in patients with prolactinomas, but its occurrence has been generally linked to poor prognosis and potential aggressive or malignant progression of the pituitary tumor ( ). Several molecular mechanisms may cause the development of resistance to DA ( ). Among them, genetic variants, intracellular signalling alterations, and the expression of the small single-stranded noncoding RNA molecules microRNA, which function in RNA silencing and posttranscriptional regulation of gene expression, may lead to a decreased number of D2DR, a decreased affinity of D2DR for DA, or altered signal transduction rising resistance to DA ( ). Particularly, a decreased mRNA stability and synthesis of D2DR resulting from genetic alterations, such as the gene variant NcoI T+, has been reported to cause resistance to DA ( ). On the other hand, estrogens may affect the balance between the short (D2S) and long (D2L) isoforms of D2DR, increasing the expression of the latter and thus limiting the effectiveness of DA ( ). Intracellular signalling may be negatively affected by cytoskeleton proteins, such as Filamin-A ( ) or β-arrestins ( , ), known to act as scaffolds for signalling molecules involved in D2DR signal transduction in lactotroph tumors and in dopaminergic neurotransmission. More recently, resistance to DA has been found associated with an increased expression of miR-93-5p ( , ) and miR-1299 ( ), or a reduced expression of miR-145 ( ). Resistance to DA may require different therapeutic approaches to be overcome. In patients resistant to a certain DA, dose escalation to maximally tolerated doses is recommended ( ), as in clinical case 3. Cabergoline doses as high as 12 mg/wk have been needed to overthrow resistance ( ). Alternatively, the switch from different DA to cabergoline may increase responsiveness to medical therapy ( ). Indeed, 6-month treatment with cabergoline at a dose range of 0.5 to 3 mg/wk has been shown to induce PRL normalization in nearly 63% and tumor shrinkage in more than 44% of patients with proven resistance to long-term bromocriptine or quinagolide ( ), thus demonstrating that patients unresponsive to different DA may benefit from chronic administration of cabergoline. Successful disease control resulted in the restoration of gonadal function in 70% of patients ( ). Nevertheless, some patients may require a multimodal therapeutic approach, including the association of medical therapy and surgery, ultimately combined with radiotherapy, particularly in presence of aggressive tumors ( , ), as in clinical case 3. Such a treatment strategy has successfully controlled 56% of patients ( ). Resistance to cabergoline represents the first clear indication for surgery in prolactinomas ( ), together with pituitary apoplexy, intolerance to DA, persistent chiasmal compression despite optimal medical therapy, cerebrospinal fluid leak while on DA, and psychiatric conditions in macroadenomas ( ). Interestingly, surgical debulking has been found to prompt a significant decrease in PRL levels while reducing the weekly cabergoline dose by 50% ( ). In experienced hands, initial remission rates with surgery were approximately 40% and 75% for macroprolactinomas and microprolactinomas, respectively, and long-term remission rates were approximately 65% and 80% for macroprolactinomas and microprolactinomas, respectively ( ). However, the improvement of surgical techniques over the years has progressively increased the successful use of neurosurgery also as a first-line treatment in prolactinomas, resulting as effective as cabergoline in patients with enclosed adenomas not located laterally from the gland and not invasive to the cavernous sinus ( ). In these patients, the surgical approach could increase cure rates and reduce the requirement of dopamine agonists for those not cured by first-line surgery, also limiting medical costs and side effects of chronic DA treatment ( ). Conversely, tumors invasive to the cavernous sinus have been reported to be associated with a higher risk of venous bleeding and a lower remission rate compared with enclosed tumors ( ). So far, surgery (83%) has been shown to provide similar outcomes compared with DA (91%) in terms of achievement of biochemical control in patients with microprolactinomas, but not in those with macroprolactinomas, in whom the rate of biochemical control is higher in medically treated (77%) compared with surgically treated (60%) patients, according to a recent meta-analysis ( ). Altogether, this evidence supports the use of surgery as a viable first-line therapeutic choice for patients with enclosed and not invasive prolactinomas and suggests an adequate tailoring of treatments based on tumor characteristics, size, and invasiveness. Radiotherapy, in any form, is now considered a third-line treatment and is reserved for those patients with macroadenomas resistant to either medical therapy or surgery, as in clinical case 3, mainly because of the long latency to therapeutic efficacy and the frequent occurrence of hypopituitarism ( ). Aggressive and malignant prolactinomas refractory to all treatment strategies may benefit from the administration of the oral alkylating chemotherapeutic agent temozolomide ( ), whose efficacy in terms of tumor growth control accounts for up to 50% of patients with prolactinomas ( ). According to the European Society survey of 166 patients, including 38 with aggressive lactotroph tumors, the use of temozolomide in aggressive prolactinomas resulted in complete regression in 5%, partial regression in 45%, stable disease in 26%, and tumor progression in 24% of cases ( ). Temozolomide is now recommended as first-line chemotherapy for aggressive pituitary tumors and pituitary carcinomas following documented tumor growth ( ). Responsiveness to temozolomide may be predicted by the evaluation of O(6)-methylguanine methyl transferase (MGMT) status by immunohistochemistry by expert neuropathologists, as high MGMT expression is generally suggestive of a lack of response ( ). Indeed, tumor regression has been documented in 46% of tumors with low MGMT expression, but only in 23.5% of those with high MGMT expression ( ). The first evaluation of the response to temozolomide should be done after the first 3 cycles ( ). If radiological progression is demonstrated, temozolomide treatment should be stopped ( ). Conversely, in patients proven to respond to first-line temozolomide after 3 cycles, treatment can be continued for at least 6 months or a longer time if a sustained therapeutic benefit is observed ( ). As for all chemotherapeutic agents, close monitoring of hematological parameters, liver function tests, and careful clinical observation should be performed for potential adverse effects (eg, fatigue, nausea, vomiting) ( ). The effectiveness of temozolomide has been shown to increase when combined with radiotherapy given its radio-sensitizing properties, thus offering a further therapeutic option for those individuals with aggressive or malignant prolactinomas ( , ). Indeed, tumor regression has been documented in 71% of patients receiving temozolomide and radiotherapy combined treatment, but only in 34% of those receiving temozolomide monotherapy ( ). Management After Treatment Withdrawal In selected cases, treatment with DA for prolactinomas may result in a complete cure and can be definitively stopped. Specifically, after bromocriptine discontinuation, persistent normoprolactinemia reportedly ranged from 7% to 44% ( ), indicating a wide variability in the long-term outcome after bromocriptine withdrawal. Recurrence of hyperprolactinemia generally occurred within 3 months after bromocriptine discontinuation ( ). However, symptomatic tumor regrowth has been reported to occur in less than 10% of cases ( , ) and to be influenced by the duration of previous DA treatment ( ). Tumor re-expansion was successfully managed by bromocriptine restarting ( ). A greater success has been demonstrated after cabergoline withdrawal ( ). Preliminary studies ( , , , ) have reported the persistence of normoprolactinemia after cabergoline withdrawal to range from 10% to 31% of patients. In a prospective study, 36 to 48 months after cabergoline discontinuation, persistent normoprolactinemia was found in 19 of 25 (76%) patients with nontumoral hyperprolactinemia, 73 of 105 (70%) of those with microprolactinomas, and in 45 of 70 (64%) of those with macroprolactinomas ( ). The median time to recurrence of hyperprolactinemia ranged from 12 to 18 months ( ). The Kaplan-Maier estimate of disease recurrence at 5 years was significantly lower in patients with nontumoral hyperprolactinemia compared with those harboring a pituitary tumor, and in patients with no evidence of tumor remnant at MRI before cabergoline withdrawal compared with those with residual tumor ( ). The role of tumor mass as the main determinant of long-term remission was confirmed by the finding that the maximal diameter during cabergoline treatment was the best predictor of the PRL level at the last follow-up visit after treatment discontinuation, with a 19% hazard rate for the recurrence of hyperprolactinemia for each millimeter increment in the maximal tumor diameter ( ). Now, the achievement of a residual tumor maximal diameter smaller than 3.1 mm in size associated with nadir PRL levels <5.4 μg/L is considered the best predictor of long-term remission from hyperprolactinemia after cabergoline withdrawal ( ). Altogether, these findings guided the advice that, after therapy with DA for at least 2 years, a trial of progressive DA dose-lowering and discontinuation can be started if PRL levels are normal and the tumor volume is evidently shrunk ( ). As shown in , the application in clinical practice of the aforementioned criteria for DA discontinuation in prolactinomas has resulted in a substantial progressive increase in the long-term remission rate after treatment withdrawal up to 75% of patients ( , , ). Nevertheless, the pooled proportion of patients with persisting normoprolactinemia after DA withdrawal was 21% in a systematic review and meta-analysis ( ), where remission rates were confirmed to be higher in idiopathic hyperprolactinemia (32%) and microprolactinomas (21%) compared with macroprolactinomas (16%). In patients with evidence of recurrence of hyperprolactinemia after treatment discontinuation, DA must be restarted. However, a second withdrawal may be attempted if patients have received cabergoline for 2 additional years ( , ). Evidence from previous studies has documented a successful outcome, defined as the achievement of normoprolactinemia, in 30% of cases ( , ). Altogether, these findings suggest that more than one-third of patients totally fulfilling the criteria for drug discontinuation may exhibit persistent normoprolactinemia over time. However, a careful follow-up after therapy withdrawal remains strongly recommended to identify as soon as possible the recurrence of hyperprolactinemia and/or tumor regrowth requiring restarting prompt treatment ( ).
